body:
What are antibiotics?

Antibiotics are medicines used to treat susceptible bacterial infections by killing bacteria or preventing their growth.

Many important antibiotics were originally discovered as substances produced by microorganisms, especially certain fungi and bacteria.

Examples include penicillin, streptomycin, tetracycline and erythromycin.

These are examples of antibiotics, not the names of microbial groups.

Discovery of penicillin

In 1928, Alexander Fleming observed that a mould growing near certain bacteria prevented their normal growth.

The mould belonged to the genus Penicillium. The antibacterial substance associated with this observation became known as penicillin.

Fleming's observation contributed to the development of one of the most important antibiotic medicines.

Antibiotics are not effective against viruses

Antibiotics act on structures or processes found in susceptible bacteria. Viruses differ from bacteria and multiply using living host cells.

Therefore, antibiotics do not directly treat ordinary viral infections such as the common cold or influenza.

A patient with a viral illness may occasionally require an antibiotic if a separate bacterial infection is also present, but the antibiotic does not eliminate the virus itself.

Why unnecessary antibiotic use is harmful

Taking antibiotics without a genuine need may expose bacteria to the medicine unnecessarily and favour the survival of bacteria that are resistant to it.

Antibiotic resistance means that certain bacteria are no longer effectively controlled by antibiotics that previously worked against them.

The resistance develops in bacteria; it is not simply the human body becoming accustomed to the medicine.

Antibiotics can also disturb beneficial bacteria naturally present in the body.

They should therefore be used only when prescribed by a qualified healthcare professional and taken according to the prescribed instructions.

Antibiotics and vaccines serve different purposes

FeatureAntibioticsVaccines
Main purposeTreat susceptible bacterial infectionsDevelop protection against specific diseases
Principal actionKill bacteria or stop bacterial growthStimulate an immune response
Usual timingWhen treatment is medically indicatedGenerally before exposure or disease
ExamplePenicillinPolio vaccine

The distinction is important because a vaccine is not simply an antibiotic given in advance. A vaccine prepares the immune system, whereas an antibiotic acts against susceptible bacteria.

Other scientists associated with microorganisms

Louis Pasteur established important scientific connections between microorganisms and fermentation. Pasteurisation, a heat-treatment process used in food preservation, is named after him.

Robert Koch identified the bacterium responsible for anthrax in 1876.

These contributions are distinct from Fleming's discovery of penicillin and Jenner's pioneering work on smallpox vaccination.

Prelims focus

  • Penicillin is associated with the fungus Penicillium.
  • Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928.
  • Antibiotics treat susceptible bacterial infections, not viral infections.
  • Louis Pasteur is associated with fermentation and pasteurisation.
  • Robert Koch identified the anthrax bacterium in 1876.
  • Trap: Antibiotic resistance develops in bacteria; vaccines and antibiotics are not interchangeable.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Ch. 2, Microorganisms: Friend and Foe, sections Medicinal Use of Microorganisms and Vaccine, pp. 20–21, 2018–19; NobelPrize.org, Sir Alexander Fleming: Biographical, account of the 1928 discovery, accessed 3 November 2026; World Health Organization, World Antibiotic Awareness Week 2019, Infections and Antibiotics; World Health Organization, Antimicrobial Resistance and COVID-19, accessed 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Penicillin acts directly against susceptible bacteria, not viruses; polio vaccine stimulates an immune response and memory for later protection.
pictures.caption: Antibiotics act against susceptible bacteria; vaccines prepare the immune system.

title: Antibiotics: Medicines Obtained from Microorganisms and Their Correct Use

body:
Why does food spoil?

Food provides nutrients that microorganisms may use for growth. When suitable microorganisms multiply in food, they can produce changes in its smell, colour, taste or texture.

For example, moist bread may develop fungal mould, and improperly stored cooked food may become spoiled through microbial activity.

Warmth, moisture, the availability of nutrients and suitable environmental conditions can favour the growth of many food-spoiling microbes.

Food spoilage and food poisoning

Food spoilage refers to undesirable changes that reduce food quality or make it unsuitable for consumption.

Food poisoning is an illness resulting from consuming contaminated food, including food containing harmful microorganisms or toxins produced by some microorganisms.

Food poisoning may cause symptoms such as vomiting, abdominal discomfort and diarrhoea.

Food that appears normal may still contain dangerous pathogens or toxins. Therefore, smell and appearance alone cannot establish that food is safe.

Principle of food preservation

Food preservation involves methods that prevent contamination, destroy harmful microorganisms or reduce conditions that permit microbial growth.

Different preservation methods work through different principles. Some use temperature, while others reduce available water, increase acidity or create protective storage conditions.

Major food preservation methods

MethodBasic principleCommon example
SaltingReduces water available for microbial growthSalted fish, raw mango
SugaringHigh sugar concentration limits available waterJam, jelly
Oil and vinegarAcidity and suitable protective conditions inhibit spoilageMango pickle
HeatingKills many microorganismsBoiled milk
RefrigerationSlows microbial multiplicationMilk, cooked food
DryingReduces moisture needed for growthDried grains
Suitable packagingReduces contamination and exposureSealed dry foods

Preservation using salt

Salt helps preserve certain foods by reducing the water available to microorganisms.

Salting has traditionally been used for fish, meat, raw mangoes and other food materials. Effective preservation depends on using an appropriate method and suitable storage conditions.

Preservation using sugar

High concentrations of sugar reduce the water available for microbial growth. This is why sugar is useful in preparing certain jams and jellies.

The presence of sugar alone does not make every food permanently safe. Preservation depends on the concentration and overall preparation and storage conditions.

Preservation using oil and vinegar

Pickles are familiar examples of preserved foods in Gujarat and many other parts of India.

Vinegar contains acetic acid, which creates conditions unfavourable for many microorganisms. Salt and suitable oil-based preparation methods may also contribute to preservation.

Oil alone does not guarantee that dangerous microorganisms cannot grow. Safe preparation, sufficient acidity or salt where required, and suitable storage remain important.

Heat treatment

Heating food can destroy many microorganisms. Boiling milk is a common household example.

Some microorganisms or their resistant forms may survive particular heating conditions. Therefore, ordinary heating and complete sterilisation should not be treated as identical processes.

Cold storage

Refrigeration slows the growth of many microorganisms. It helps perishable food remain usable for a longer period when correctly stored.

However, refrigeration does not necessarily kill all microorganisms. Some can survive, and certain microorganisms may still grow slowly at low temperatures.

Pasteurisation of milk

Pasteurisation is a controlled heat-treatment process used to reduce harmful microorganisms in foods such as milk.

The process is named after Louis Pasteur.

In a common short-time milk pasteurisation method, milk is heated to approximately 72°C for 15 seconds and then rapidly cooled. Other recognised time-and-temperature combinations also exist.

The Class 8 textbook describes the principle using approximately 70°C for 15–30 seconds followed by rapid cooling. The exact conditions depend on the pasteurisation method.

Pasteurisation greatly improves milk safety but does not necessarily eliminate every microorganism. Ordinary pasteurised milk generally requires appropriate refrigerated storage.

Heating: Destroys many microorganisms.
Refrigeration: Primarily slows microbial multiplication.
Pasteurisation: Uses controlled heating and cooling to reduce harmful microbes.
Salting and sugaring: Restrict the water available for microbial growth.

Connecting useful and harmful microorganisms

The same broad groups of microorganisms can have different effects depending on the organism and the conditions.

  • Bacteria: Lactobacillus helps form curd, Rhizobium fixes nitrogen, and certain bacteria cause cholera.
  • Fungi: Yeast helps bread rise, decomposer fungi recycle organic matter, and other fungi cause wheat rust.
  • Protozoa: Some are harmless free-living organisms, while Plasmodium causes malaria.
  • Algae and cyanobacteria: Photosynthetic forms contribute to food production in ecosystems, while some cyanobacteria also fix nitrogen.
  • Viruses: They reproduce inside living host cells and include the agents causing polio and dengue.
  • Vaccination: Stimulates protective immune responses against particular diseases.

Prelims focus

  • Salt and concentrated sugar inhibit many microbes by reducing available water.
  • Vinegar contains acetic acid and helps preserve pickles.
  • Refrigeration slows microbial growth but does not reliably sterilise food.
  • Pasteurisation is associated with Louis Pasteur.
  • A common short-time milk pasteurisation condition is 72°C for 15 seconds followed by rapid cooling.
  • Trap: Food can contain harmful microorganisms or toxins even when visible signs of spoilage are absent.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Ch. 2, Microorganisms: Friend and Foe, sections Food Poisoning and Food Preservation, pp. 25–26, 2018–19; GCERT, Science, Std. 8, Ch. 2, pp. 25–26; Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, Milk and Milk Product Processing, audit items 23–24, p. 2, 2020; World Health Organization, How Do Vaccines Work, sections on immune response and protection, accessed 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Refrigeration slows microbial growth; heating kills many microbes. Salt, sugar and vinegar limit growth. Milk pasteurisation uses about 72°C for 15 seconds, then rapid cooling.
pictures.caption: Food preservation works by reducing microbial contamination, survival or growth.
